answers.answer: Only the order of the documents changes, so that the document containing the answer sits in a different position. The question, the set of distractor documents, and the amount of text stay the same, because input context length is controlled separately by changing the number of documents. With one variable moving, a difference in accuracy between two runs has a single candidate cause, which is position. Change distractors or length at the same time and the resulting number is about several things at once.
accept: says the only change is the position of the answer-bearing document, achieved by reordering the documents
says the question, the other documents, and the context length are held fixed, with length controlled separately by the number of documents
says isolating one variable is what makes the accuracy difference attributable to position

answers.answer: The reference point is the closed-book setting, answering with no input documents at all, which scored 56.1 percent. With the relevant information in the middle, performance fell below that, and in the worst case the 20-document and 30-document settings were lower than performance with no documents. It is worse than an ordinary drop because retrieval had negative value: supplying the correct passage left the system behind where it would have been supplying nothing.
accept: identifies the closed-book or no-documents setting as the reference point
gives 56.1 percent as its value
explains that retrieval made the system worse than no retrieval, so the retrieval stage subtracted value rather than adding it

answers.answer: In multi-document QA the model either failed to locate the relevant passage in its context or located it and failed to reason from it, and the task cannot separate those. Key-value retrieval rules out the comprehension explanation: the input is a serialized JSON object of key-value pairs where every key and value is a unique randomly generated UUID, so there is nothing to understand, no distractor is more topically related than another, and the correct output is a copy of a string already in the prompt. A failure there is a failure to find a token, not to understand one.
accept: names the two competing explanations for a multi-document QA failure, locating the passage versus reasoning over it
says the key-value inputs are randomly generated UUID keys and values with no semantic content
concludes that a key-value failure can only be a retrieval or locating failure, not a comprehension failure

answers.answer: On key-value retrieval it improved performance dramatically, with all models reaching near-perfect scores. On multi-document question answering it minimally affected the performance trends. One intervention with two outcomes is information about the two tasks rather than a single verdict to average out: it addresses whatever the synthetic probe isolates, and whatever else makes mid-context documents hard in QA is untouched. Before adopting a probe-validated mitigation, measure it on the task you actually run.
accept: says key-value retrieval improved dramatically, to near-perfect for all models
says multi-document QA was affected minimally
draws the conclusion that a fix validated on a synthetic probe is not established on the real task and has to be measured there

answers.answer: If the bias came from what the documents said, shuffling the documents would carry the attention peaks along with them and the U shape would move or disappear. The pattern persists after random shuffling instead, which is evidence that the bias does not depend on the documents' actual content and belongs to the positions themselves: tokens at the beginning and the end of the input receive higher attention regardless of relevance.
accept: says a content-driven bias would move with the documents under shuffling
says the U-shaped pattern persisted after random shuffling
concludes the bias is positional rather than content-dependent, with start and end tokens attended more regardless of relevance

answers.answer: The attention measurement is a claim about particular trained models, scoped to what was tested: two multi-document QA tasks and the two models used, Vicuna-7b-v1.5-16k and tulu-2-7b. The structural argument is a claim about the model class, that lost-in-the-middle-type behaviour can arise from the architecture of causal Transformers itself, with causal masking and residual connections inducing broad, often U-shaped influence profiles at finite depth. You check the first by measuring attention in more models; you check the second by whether the profiles the theory predicts match measured input-token influence, which is the comparison its authors report.
accept: says the attention finding is scoped to the specific trained models and tasks measured
says the structural claim is about causal Transformer architecture as a class, naming causal masking and residual connections
distinguishes the checks: measure more models versus compare predicted influence profiles against measured input-token influence

answers.answer: First, the effect is not present in every model or every configuration: evaluated inside its 2048-token training-time context window, Flan-UL2 was relatively robust to position, with 1.9 percent absolute difference between best and worst case, so there was almost nothing for a reranker to recover. Second, the direction is not universal: position bias is primarily model-driven, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek 7B Chat, and Mistral 7B consistently favour late positions, against the common assumption of an early-token preference, so first place is not always the strong slot. The rule is a hypothesis about a specific model, to be settled by running the position sweep.
accept: cites Flan-UL2 within its 2048-token training-time window as relatively robust, with about 1.9 percent between best and worst case
cites the models that consistently favour late positions, against an assumed universal early-token preference
concludes the placement rule has to be measured per model rather than assumed
